column2: No obstruction, clear CXR and a slightly low TLCO with normal KCO (small alveolar volume) point to obesity as the cause of breathlessness.
Upper-lobe cavitating pneumonia in an alcohol-dependent inpatient is classically Klebsiella pneumoniae ('redcurrant jelly' sputum).
C. psittaci is intracellular, so beta-lactams fail: switch to doxycycline 100 mg bd for 10–14 days (macrolide if pregnant).
Ataxia and slurred speech after ascent is high-altitude cerebral oedema: descend immediately and give dexamethasone (and oxygen).
Pink frothy sputum and crackles at altitude is HAPE: descent, oxygen and nifedipine to lower pulmonary artery pressure.
A fall in VC > 20–25% from upright to supine indicates diaphragm weakness — here phrenic palsy after cardiac surgery.
Fluctuating diplopia with breathlessness in a young woman suggests myasthenia gravis; antibodies, EMG and CT for thymoma.
Unilateral hyperlucent emphysematous lung is Swyer–James (MacLeod) syndrome after childhood obliterative bronchiolitis.
Clubbing is not a feature of chronic bronchitis/COPD; it occurs in cancer, fibrosis, asbestosis and chronic suppurative lung disease.
OSA is 2–3 times commoner in men, so female gender is the least frequent feature listed.
Isolated low TLCO with normal volumes suggests pulmonary vascular disease, e.g. arteriovenous malformation (HHT); bubble echo or CTPA.
Chronic productive cough after childhood measles with clubbing and coarse crackles is bronchiectasis; HRCT confirms.
Haemoptysis, anaemia and a fixed localised wheeze with gynaecomastia (ectopic hCG) is bronchial carcinoma.
Sudden pink frothy sputum, bilateral crackles, cold peripheries and hypotension is cardiogenic pulmonary oedema with shock.
Fever, rusty sputum and pleuritic pain with dullness and bronchial breathing is lobar pneumonia (pneumococcal).
Fever, cough and breathlessness 4–8 h after work in a farmer is acute extrinsic allergic alveolitis (farmer's lung).
Stony dullness with absent breath sounds is a pleural effusion; with fever and sweats in a young person, likely tuberculous.
Sudden pleuritic pain with hyper-resonance and absent breath sounds in a young man is primary spontaneous pneumothorax.
Post-operative hypoxaemia, raised JVP and hypotension with a clear chest is massive PE: systemic thrombolysis.
Hypotension, pulsus paradoxus, raised JVP and soft heart sounds days after MI is tamponade (free-wall rupture).
Exertional syncope with S4, basal ejection murmur and apical MR murmur in a young athlete is HOCM.
Recurrent cough and breathlessness with widespread wheeze and a normal CXR is asthma; confirm variable obstruction.
A left atrial mass obstructing the mitral valve with syncope and clubbing is atrial myxoma; excise surgically.
Fever with a new regurgitant murmur and clubbing suggests subacute infective endocarditis; blood cultures and echo.
Swinging fever, pleuritic pain and stony dullness with clubbing is empyema; aspirate (pus, pH < 7.2) and drain.
Chronic purulent sputum with clubbing, crackles and infertility is bronchiectasis (CF or ciliary dyskinesia).
Progressive dry cough with clubbing and bilateral Velcro crackles is idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
Clubbing (thyroid acropachy) with exophthalmos and pretibial myxoedema is specific to Graves' disease.
Resonant silent hemithorax with hypotension after trauma is tension pneumothorax: decompress, then chest tube.
PaO2 < 8 kPa with a normal PaCO2 despite maximal asthma therapy means tiring: ICU for intubation and ventilation.
Sudden breathlessness with RV strain and SBP < 90 in a bed-bound patient is massive PE: alteplase.
Dry cough, clubbing and fine crackles is IPF; pirfenidone or nintedanib slows FVC decline.
Itch, facial/tongue swelling and wheeze after a new drug is anaphylaxis: IM adrenaline 0.5 mg, repeat after 5 min if needed.
Dry cough after starting antihypertensive treatment with a normal CXR is ACE-inhibitor cough; switch to an ARB.
Persistent fever with a turbid effusion of pH 7.0 after pneumonia is empyema: chest drain plus antibiotics.
A persistent hilar opacity with bloody sputum in a heavy smoker suggests central carcinoma: CT, then bronchoscopy and biopsy.
Chronic cough, sweats, weight loss and apical opacities is TB: sputum for AFB smear, culture and NAAT.
Ischaemic pain with ST depression: high-sensitivity troponin to separate NSTEMI from unstable angina.
Nocturnal cough after moving house in an atopic non-smoker suggests cough-variant asthma: spirometry with reversibility (± FeNO).
Paroxysmal headache, palpitations and sweating with hypertension and postural drop suggest phaeochromocytoma: metanephrines.
Nocturnal breathlessness with frothy sputum in IHD is acute pulmonary oedema: IV furosemide (plus nitrates if BP allows).
Post-operative PE with SBP > 90 is not high-risk: anticoagulate with heparin; thrombolysis only for shock.
Restriction (FVC 60%, ratio ~0.88) with clubbing is IPF; pirfenidone is recommended at FVC 50–80%.
Absent air entry with the mediastinum shifted away and hypotension after trauma is tension pneumothorax: decompress and drain.
HFrEF on furosemide and aspirin with BP 165/95: add an ACE inhibitor (lisinopril) for survival and BP.
New COPD with exertional breathlessness: start an as-needed short-acting bronchodilator (salbutamol), stop smoking, rehab.
Infective COPD exacerbation: 28% oxygen, nebulised salbutamol + ipratropium, prednisolone and oral amoxicillin.
COPD exacerbation with persistent acidosis (pH 7.28, PaCO2 9.4) despite treatment: non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP).
Stable PaO2 6.5 kPa twice in a non-smoker with COPD: long-term oxygen therapy (≥ 15 h/day) improves survival.
COPD still symptomatic on short-acting bronchodilators: add a LABA + LAMA inhaler.
Pink frothy sputum with a gallop rhythm is acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema.
Haemoptysis then crescentic GN with linear IgG on the GBM is anti-GBM (Goodpasture's) disease.
Nasal obstruction then haemoptysis with multiple nodules is granulomatosis with polyangiitis (c-ANCA).
Fever, sweats, weight loss and haemoptysis with AFB on ZN stain is pulmonary TB.
Collapse with haemoptysis and pleuritic pain after a long flight, with RV strain on ECG, is PE.
Heart failure gives a transudate (protein and LDH ratios below Light's thresholds, few cells), often bilateral; treat with diuretics.
Pain and surgical emphysema after vomiting is Boerhaave rupture: left effusion with pH ~6, food particles and high amylase.
Turbid neutrophilic fluid with pH < 7.2 and very low glucose not responding to antibiotics is empyema: chest drain.
Pancreatitis causes a left-sided exudate with very high pleural amylase.
A bloody high-LDH exudate with atypical mesothelial cells after asbestos exposure suggests mesothelioma; pleural biopsy.
